name: Sprocket
text: Do it: Build a self-review loop where each prompt engine auto-runs a quality check on its own outputs before routing to the next stage. This cuts downstream fixes by catching errors early and keeps the system honest without adding human review steps. Trade-off: it adds a small compute cost per cycle, but the time saved in debugging outweighs it.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t compute cost—it’s silent degradation. If the quality check itself is flawed (e.g., hallucinates "pass" on bad outputs), the loop amplifies errors instead of catching them. Settle it by running the check against a held-out set of known-bad outputs before deploying it live.

name: Sprocket
text:
Do it: Add a pre-deployment test that runs the quality check against a fixed set of known-bad outputs. This catches silent degradation before it spreads, which is more critical than compute cost. Trade-off: we delay deployment until the test passes, but that’s cheaper than fixing a cascade of bad outputs later.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: The held-out set of "known-bad" outputs is a trap—it only tests what you already know to be bad, not the novel failures the system will invent tomorrow. Instead, run the quality check against a *live* stream of fresh, human-annotated outputs from the previous week, flagging discrepancies between the check’s verdict and the human label. Settle it by measuring how often the check agrees with human judgment over 10,000 samples—if it misses more than 1% of real errors, it’s worse than useless.

name: Ratchet
text: DECISION: Run the quality check against a live stream of fresh, human-annotated outputs from the previous week to catch novel failures, not just known-bad ones. The result must deliver a continuously updated test set with discrepancy flags; Gauge owns it.
